Nvidia, Alphabet, Microsoft, and Micron Are All Buying Anthropic’s IPO. Should You Buy Too?
sum: - Anthropic provided a price range for its IPO, valuing the business at $1.4 trillion at the high end.
- Growing concerns about AI companies have weighed on its valuation.
- Anthropic is showing good progress scaling the business, but it needs more capital.

Anthropic is set to be one of the biggest IPOs in history. The frontier AI lab revealed plans to sell 825 million shares of Class A stock at a share price between $70 and $78. At the high end of that range, it'll raise $64 billion and imply a fully diluted valuation of $1.4 trillion.

Separately, Anthropic is raising $26 billion in a private placement of the company's Class N shares, which carry no voting rights (but convert to Class A shares if sold to an unaffiliated buyer). That share class allows strategic business partners, including Alphabet(NASDAQ:GOOG)(NASDAQ:GOOGL), Nvidia(NASDAQ:NVDA), Microsoft(NASDAQ:MSFT), Micron Techology(NASDAQ:MU), and others, to invest in the company without conflict of interest. Indeed, all four companies are on the roster of investors in the private placement, buying shares at the same price as the IPO.

Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The question investors need to ask is: Are the big tech companies getting yet another deal on Anthropic shares? And if so, should you join them now that average investors finally have an opportunity to buy the stock?

Micron's Contracted Revenue Backs a Bull Case, but Wall Street Won't Commit
sum: Micron Technology is drawing a split verdict from the analyst community, even as its shares push higher. The stock rose 4.6% to €678.60 in pre-market trading today, extending a recovery that began Monday when memory-chip names rallied alongside SanDisk following the prior week's selloff, which had been driven by worries over AI data-center construction.
The rebound has company. Asian semiconductor stocks climbed today on strong AI-chip demand, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both posting gains, according to AP.

Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider lifted his view of Micron's risk-reward balance today but kept his "Neutral" rating intact. His price target stands at $1,250. The more constructive stance rests on expectations of hefty free cash flow in coming quarters and a valuation close to tangible book value — meaning the case only holds if Micron actually delivers that cash.

KeyBanc's John Vinh took a bolder line yesterday, reaffirming a $1,750 target built on six times his earnings estimate for fiscal 2028. That math assumes unusually high profits persist well beyond the next quarterly report. Goldman's neutral call, despite the improved setup, reflects a more guarded read. Both views converge on the same variable: the money Micron ultimately earns.

Underpinning the bull argument is a shift in how Micron sells. The company says it holds 26 multi-year take-or-pay agreements covering more than 35% of revenue through 2030. Over 75% of its 2027 production is already committed. That gives the memory maker a concrete planning edge — provided customers take the promised volumes on the expected terms.

For investors, the durability of those commitments matters more than a single low earnings multiple. A cheap price-to-earnings ratio only convinces when the underlying profits can hold up over time, and that is precisely where the customer contracts face their test.

Separately, Micron is managing a labor dispute at its Fab 11E site in Taoyuan, Taiwan. Bloomberg reported roughly a week ago that construction work there had been halted over a conflict about profit-sharing.

sum: On November 5 ET, Micron shares plunged 17.46% to $656.39 amid broad semiconductor sector weakness, regulatory concerns over data center expansion, and a paused plant project in Taiwan. The stock has fallen over 30% from its October peak, breaking below key moving averages and forming a death cross. While the RSI indicates oversold conditions near 27.1, hinting at a potential technical rebound toward $700–$737.88 if the $650 support holds, the broader short-term trend remains bearish, with downside risks extending toward the $450–$500 range if support fails.

TradingKey - On November 5 ET, Micron (MU) shares tumbled, closing down 17.46% at around $656.39 after touching an intraday low of $650, marking a nearly six-month low. Trading volume surged to approximately 75 million shares, more than double its recent average. Since hitting $990 on October 28, Micron has pulled back more than 30% cumulatively and sequentially broken below multiple key moving averages, further expanding its short-term correction.

Micron's sharp drop yesterday was primarily driven by broad-based weakness across the AI and semiconductor sectors. Following the U.S. midterm elections, the market began focusing on potential tightening of approvals, as well as power and water restrictions, on data center construction in certain states. If the pace of data center construction slows, the growth momentum of demand for server DRAM, HBM, and enterprise storage could also be affected. Such concerns dragged memory stocks lower across the board, with SanDisk, SK Hynix, and others all recording double-digit declines yesterday.

In addition, news that Micron paused a memory chip plant construction project in Taiwan added to the stock's volatility. Meanwhile, although the recent continuous rise in memory prices benefits memory chipmakers' selling prices, it has also begun putting pressure on costs and demand for end-device manufacturers such as PC and smartphone makers, prompting the market to reassess the duration of the current memory upcycle.

Looking at Micron's daily chart, the stock broke below the July 29 low of $737.88 on Thursday, shifting the overall candlestick structure from high-level consolidation into a deeper downturn and significantly strengthening bearish market momentum.

sum: Micron (NASDAQ:MU), Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK), and SK hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) are continuing their climb after Tuesday's closing bell, following a solid regular session that saw their shares rise 2.6%, 4.8%, and 2.1%, respectively. With AMD and Super Micro Computer delivering encouraging earnings after trading ended, investors have another reason to believe AI infrastructure spending remains healthy.

AMD reported a 97% jump in data-center revenue to $8.5 billion, while Super Micro's quarterly sales nearly quadrupled to $19.95 billion. The server manufacturer also raised its annual revenue outlook to as much as $82 billion, suggesting customers aren't slowing purchases of computing equipment. Such developments offer encouragement for memory manufacturers supplying essential components to these systems.

Micron is working to protect itself against the unpredictable pricing cycles that have historically troubled memory-chip manufacturers. The company has expanded its portfolio of long-term customer agreements to 26, up from 16 just three months earlier, with contracts now covering more than 35% of projected revenue through 2030. Many include minimum pricing commitments, while newer deals reflect higher market prices, potentially helping Micron maintain stronger profit margins even when the industry eventually cools.

Meanwhile, Micron's next-generation HBM4 production continues expanding, with the manufacturer already securing agreements for the vast majority of its planned 2027 high-bandwidth memory supply at significantly higher prices. The company is also working with Nvidia on customized HBM4E technology for future AI processors, potentially strengthening its position in a market where customers are competing for limited production capacity.

And the shortage could last longer than investors previously expected, with Micron anticipating tighter DRAM and NAND supply conditions during 2027 and 2028. More than 75% of its output for next year has already been committed, while customers are discussing purchases extending into 2031. That gives the manufacturer greater visibility into future sales, although expanding production capacity will require heavy investment.

items.t: Better Buy: Micron or Nvidia Stock
sum: Two of the hottest stocks on the market are Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and Micron (NASDAQ: MU). Both companies are thriving on heightened data center demand, and each has integral products for the artificial intelligence (AI) training ecosystem. Nvidia makes graphics processing units (GPUs), while Micron makes memory chips. That makes these two partners rather than competitors.
However, there can only be one stock that's the better buy between them. So, which one is it?

In the GPU world, Nvidia stands on top. Its ecosystem and hardware are better than the competition's, making it the top choice for any company looking to build out its AI model. There is a lot that differentiates Nvidia's products from rivals, so it has earned a premium as a result.

Micron is a bit different. There isn't a whole lot to separate one memory manufacturer from another, which results in a commoditized market. When demand is high and supply is low, as it is now, memory prices soar. That's exactly what we're seeing, and it's powering Micron's stock to new heights.

The issue is that this memory shortage won't last forever. Micron and its peers are all building new fabrication facilities to meet demand. Eventually, demand will slow or decrease, or supply will catch up and cause memory prices to crater.
Once that occurs, it will return Micron's business to the flatline state that it once was. That will be a painful day for shareholders.
Nvidia is certainly thriving off of component shortage, but its pricing isn't nearly as affected by overall demand as Micron's. As a result, I'm giving the business edge to Nvidia.

The rally is driven by surging demand and a shortage of high-bandwidth memory, the specialized chips that sit alongside AI accelerators in data centers. Hyperscalers, including Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOG), and Meta (META), are projected to spend roughly $700 billion on AI infrastructure this year, and memory is a critical input at every stage of that build-out. The stock also might appear like a steal trading at a mere 14x estimated FY ’26 earnings and 8x next year’s earnings. See MU valuation metrics However, the memory markets are extremely cyclical. So how has the stock reacted in past crashes?
While cloud compute has driven much of AI demand, the edge may be next. See how Qualcomm could be one of the biggest beneficiaries.

The memory industry has produced multiple severe price collapses in the past fifteen years, all sharing the same underlying cause. Building a new DRAM fabrication facility takes two to three years and costs tens of billions of dollars. Once built, the economics strongly favor running it at maximum capacity regardless of the prevailing price. Demand surges, prices spike, manufacturers commit to new capacity, and by the time that capacity comes online, the market it was built for no longer exists.

The 2022-2023 Memory Crash: The 2022 to 2023 downturn was one of the most severe in financial terms. Post-pandemic demand evaporated. Supplier inventories reached 31 weeks by early 2023. Micron reported a GAAP net loss of $2.31 billion in a single quarter, its largest ever; cut its workforce by 10%; and sharply reduced its capital budget. The stock declined roughly 50% from early 2022 levels and traded at about 11x forward earnings at its peak.

The 2018-2019 Inventory Unwind: During 2018 and 2019, cloud operators over-ordered memory through 2017, then steadily reduced purchases through 2018 as inventories swelled. NAND prices fell roughly 60% and DRAM approximately 40%.

As many investors know by now, AI infrastructure requires a massive amount of computer chips to train and operate. In the early days of AI growth, this was mainly the high-powered GPUs sold by Nvidia. Now, high-bandwidth memory chips are getting in on the party because of the need for rapid data transfers between data centers.

This has led to demand greatly outstripping supply, giving manufacturers like Micron -- one of the few memory chip makers in the world -- immense pricing power when selling to AI infrastructure builders. items.t: Where Will Micron Stock Be in 5 Years?
sum: For the last few decades, Micron Technology (MU +6.25%) has been a laggard in the U.S. technology industry -- struggling to surpass the highs it achieved during the dot-com bubble in 2000. However, everything changed with the arrival of generative artificial intelligence (AI), which has led to a surge in demand for its high-bandwidth memory chips (HBM).

The new demand has sent Micron's shares up 330% in the last 12 months alone. And the rally is expected to continue as memory chip shortages allow it to charge higher prices to consumers. That said, investors shouldn't expect the boom times to last forever. And Micron will need to translate its near-term success into long-term shareholder value. Let's dig deeper into what the next five years could have in store.

To understand Micron's future, we must first look at its past. Since its founding in 1978, the company has supplied computer memory and storage devices like DRAM and NAND flash. These are used in everything from personal computers to automobiles and cellphones. That said, despite having a wide range of use cases, memory hardware has historically been a punishing industry for long-term investors.

The industry's main challenge is cyclicality because computer memory hardware is highly commoditized. Chips produced by Micron won't be very functionally different from chips made by its rivals in China or South Korea. Couple this fact with high fixed costs and long manufacturing lead times, and you have the ingredients for consistent boom-and-bust cycles due to regular mismatches between memory supply and demand.

Micron has often delivered strong results despite these challenges. But it usually has a lower valuation compared to other technology companies because investors can be hesitant to invest in a company whose growth and margins could suddenly erode due to oversupply.

Generative AI has supercharged demand for computer memory. These devices are needed to store the vast amount of training data for large language models (LLMs), as well as provide the "working memory" for inference as they shift through trained data to answer user queries.
The industry may be experiencing its biggest boom cycle yet, with analysts expecting AI data centers to consume a whopping 70% of memory chip production in 2026.

items.t: Micron stock soars on earnings beat amid 'unprecedented' AI-fueled demand for memory chips
sum: Micron (MU) stock soared more than 10% Thursday after its quarterly results showed the memory chipmaker thriving thanks to the tech industry's rush to build data centers that can power artificial intelligence.

Micron's high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips — a type of DRAM, or dynamic random access memory — are a crucial part of AI server systems, storing data temporarily and rapidly feeding it to GPUs (graphics processing units) as they train and run AI models. The company is a major supplier of memory to AI chip giant Nvidia (NVDA).
Micron's DRAM revenue rose 69% to $10.8 billion in the company's first quarter, driven by AI-linked demand for HBM.

That upswing helped Micron's first quarter earnings and revenue surpass Wall Street's expectations, with its EPS of $4.78 above the projected $3.95 and its $13.6 billion in quarterly revenue above the roughly $13 billion estimated by Wall Street analysts tracked by Bloomberg.
Revenue from Micron's NAND — or storage chips — used in data centers surpassed $1 billion for the first time.

Micron was more bullish than expected about the future, forecasting revenue between $18.3 billion and $19.1 billion in the second quarter, above the $14.4 billion expected. The chipmaker's profits are also set to benefit as surging AI demand has created an industry shortage of memory chips: The company sees EPS hitting $8.42 at the midpoint in the February quarter, ahead of the $4.71 estimated by analysts, and projects its gross margin will hit an all-time high of 68%.

"Over the last few months, our customers' AI data center build-out plans have driven a sharp increase in demand forecast for memory and storage," CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said in a call with analysts following the results Wednesday. "We believe that the aggregate industry supply will remain substantially short of the demand for the foreseeable future."

items.t: Will Data Center AI Chip Demand Keep Aiding Micron's Sales Growth?
High-Bandwidth Memory Stocks: The Limiting Factor to the AI Boom?
sum: Artificial intelligence (“AI”) isn’t “born” smart. Its “intelligence” relies on what it’s taught and the quality of that “education.”

The volume of data necessary to teach AI models is massive. For instance, GPT-3 – an earlier version of OpenAI’s ChatGPT – is estimated to have trained on 45 terabytes of data. That’s more than four times all the information contained in the U.S. Library of Congress.

But, just like a human, an AI model also needs to “remember” what it has learned. And the amount of memory that AI systems currently employ to process this data is insufficient. This is causing a major bottleneck – slower speeds and less efficiency – in AI model training and deployment. And that must be addressed quickly to keep up with demand from users during this AI boom.

Fortunately, a few tech companies have the products to address this. And two pureplay memory companies that should be on your radar are Micron Technology (MU) and SK hynix (A000660 KOSE). Both are known for fast, high-bandwidth memory (“HBM”) chips to ease the bottleneck and allow AI to perform tasks at much faster rates.
But this technology doesn’t just maintain the momentum of the AI boom. HBM is completely revolutionizing AI performance. Let’s examine how.

The widening gap between processor speed and memory bandwidth – and the reason for the bottleneck – is called the AI memory wall. This occurs when processors wait too long for data from memory, resulting in a significant lag in AI performance. It’s a bit like if you, a human, struggle to remember an important detail. You have to pause and think before continuing with whatever task you’re on.

This bottleneck is caused by one thing. Processor performance has improved exponentially. But memory performance and speed haven’t kept up. Even when using the most powerful processors, AI applications still lose efficiency because the memory isn’t feeding them the data they need to perform optimally.
